stories.headline: Update: CENTCOM Commander Briefs Trump on Iran Naval Blockade as Dual-Track Strategy Continues
stories.summary:
Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, briefed President Trump on Thursday on the state of the Iran war, with a focus on the ongoing naval blockade, according to two U.S. officials cited by Axios. The briefing came as the administration pursues two tracks at once: seeking a deal to restart peace talks while preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations after the midterm elections.

Axios noted that Trump followed a similar pattern before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in February, pairing diplomacy with military preparation. Qatar-led mediators have been working on a deal to restart U.S.-Iran talks and avert renewed fighting.

Separately, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said four tankers struck naval mines after using what it called unauthorized routes through the Strait of Hormuz. The claim, which was not independently verified in the reporting, points to continued risk for commercial shipping in a key energy corridor.

The briefing follows the firing of Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the Pentagon's top military planner, whom Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed this week over alleged leaks of classified information about Iran and Ukraine. The Pentagon has put the cost of the Iran war at more than $47 billion. No decision on resuming major operations has been announced.

stories.headline: Binance Investigates Suspected Crypto Hack That Could Total $5.7 Billion
stories.summary:
Crypto exchange Binance said it is investigating what could be the largest cryptocurrency hack in history, after users saw as much as $5.7 billion in funds drained from wallets on Thursday afternoon. The company described the incident as a "security issue" and temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while it conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement.

Other cryptocurrency firms froze about $3 billion in assets in response, the company said. Binance vowed to cover all user losses. The exact mechanism of the breach and the identity of those responsible have not been disclosed.

Axios reported that the suspected hack follows a wave of high-profile cyberattacks and data breaches during what has been called "Black October," when a series of hacks and AI-discovered software bugs raised fears of a broader global crisis. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who is no longer an executive at the company, also commented on the situation.

If confirmed at the reported scale, the theft would far exceed previous record crypto heists and could shake confidence in major exchanges. Binance has not said when withdrawals will resume.

stories.headline: Democrats Favored to Retake House as Parties Pour Final Spending Into 70 Districts Ahead of Nov. 3
stories.summary:
With Election Day on Nov. 3, an NPR analysis found 70 House districts where both Democrats and Republicans are each spending more than six figures on advertising in the final days, including some in deep red territory. The Associated Press will tabulate results in nearly 7,000 races, including congressional, state legislative and gubernatorial contests.

Axios reported that polls point to a decisive Democratic victory and that party members feel "nauseously optimistic," in the words of one House Democrat, while fearing a large polling error or a late disaster. Republicans are defending their majority and have argued that local issues and turnout can outperform national polling.

States are preparing for the vote, some under new congressional maps and voting rules, alongside routine election security measures. Prediction markets have also drawn scrutiny: Sens. Elizabeth Warren and a Republican colleague pressed Kalshi and Polymarket about insider trading and manipulation, Polymarket paused trading after a security incident that drained $2.65 million from user wallets, and Utah filed felony counts against Kalshi and its founders under state gambling laws.

Results from the contested districts will determine control of the House for the remainder of the term.

stories.headline: Farmers Squeezed by High Fuel Costs Despite Administration Relief Efforts
stories.summary:
Farmers are facing sharply higher operating costs because of elevated fuel prices, even as the Trump administration takes steps to ease the burden. Missouri Farm Bureau President Garrett Hawkins said harvest is costing nearly twice as much this season, adding, "Everything is tied back to energy."

Earlier this month President Trump signed an order allowing greater access to tax-exempt red dyed diesel, normally reserved for off-road uses such as farm equipment. Thirty-one states have temporarily relaxed restrictions, and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins on Thursday urged the rest to follow and asked states with waivers to extend them through at least Dec. 31. Hawkins said some farmers may hesitate to use dyed fuel on roads because of uncertainty over how long traces remain in tanks and how long regulators will show leniency.

The administration has also announced an $8 billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program. Hawkins called it a positive acknowledgment of the problem but noted it will initially apply only to row crops, excluding for example livestock haulers, with other commodities to be announced later. USDA is expected to release details on distribution.

stories.headline: Trump Warns House Democrats Against Impeaching Hegseth
stories.summary:
President Trump on Thursday cautioned congressional Democrats against impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth if they win the House next week. Asked by the Washington Examiner before leaving for a South Carolina rally, he said, "All they do is they talk about impeaching everybody," and added that "if we wanted to play that game, we could play it just as well." He praised Hegseth as "a great warrior" and "the best at his job in many, many years." It was unclear what retaliation he meant, though he has previously threatened to veto all legislation from a Democratic-led Congress.

House Democrats filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April, led by Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona, citing the Iran war, which began Feb. 28 and has pushed up gas and diesel prices, and the lethal boat strikes against alleged drug traffickers. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who is leaving Congress in January after losing his primary, said he will force a vote on impeachment articles when the House returns after the election, accusing Hegseth of illegal conduct in Iran and other campaigns.

The warning comes as Cook Political Report rates 220 seats as at least lean Democratic against 198 for Republicans, with 17 toss-ups. Hegseth also fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, this week over alleged leaks of classified information about Iran and Ukraine. Republicans generally defend Hegseth's conduct of the war and drug-strike campaign as lawful and necessary, while Democrats call them unauthorized and costly.

stories.headline: Nvidia Rejects Report That Executive Tied to CEO Jensen Huang Passed Intelligence to Beijing
stories.summary:
Nvidia on Thursday dismissed a New York Times report that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset. The Times reported that American spy agencies discovered last year that Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, funneled information to Beijing. She is described as a businesswoman who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang.

According to the report, President Trump was briefed on the findings and took no action. Nvidia said the chip diversion allegations were "thoroughly investigated and debunked last year."

The report arrives amid sustained scrutiny of advanced AI chip sales and possible diversion to China, a central issue in U.S.-China technology competition. Critics of the administration's approach to chip exports are likely to seize on the claim that no action followed the briefing, while Nvidia and supporters of looser export policy maintain that its compliance has been vetted. The government has not publicly detailed its assessment.

stories.headline: Patrick Stewart, Star of Stage and 'Star Trek,' Dies at 86
stories.summary:
Patrick Stewart, the classically trained British actor who brought Shakespearean gravitas to "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and the "X-Men" films, died Wednesday in Los Angeles at 86. His spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, said he died after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia, diagnoses that had not been previously disclosed.

Best known as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard and Professor Charles Xavier, Stewart spent much of his career on stage. He played roles from Claudius to Macbeth, performed a one-man "A Christmas Carol," and appeared with friend Ian McKellen in Pinter's "No Man's Land" and Beckett's "Waiting for Godot." His 2008 Broadway Macbeth earned his only Tony nomination.

Raised in a working-class family in Mirfield, Yorkshire, he won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. In his memoir "Making It So," he wrote about his father's violence toward his mother, and he later became a patron of the domestic abuse charity Refuge.

stories.headline: Russian Strikes Kill 19 Civilians Across Ukraine, Including 14 at Dnipro Rail Station
stories.summary:
Russian airstrikes across Ukraine killed 19 civilians on Thursday, according to reports. The deadliest attack came when a Russian drone hit two trains at a station in central Ukraine, killing at least 14 people. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strikes demonstrated Moscow's "true attitude towards de-escalation" of the war.

The attacks came as a local truce, credited to Melania Trump, brought some hope elsewhere in the country. That truce is in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. The contrast underscores the uneven picture of de-escalation efforts as diplomatic contacts continue.

The strikes also coincide with new diplomatic outreach involving Russia. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare phone call with Vladimir Putin this week on the war in Ukraine. Putin welcomed the call and said Moscow supports efforts to restore ties with Europe after years of confrontation. Whether those contacts produce any movement toward a ceasefire remains unclear, and Kyiv has pointed to the continued attacks on civilian infrastructure as evidence that Russia is not serious about de-escalation.

stories.headline: Update: Alaska Governor Orders Probe, House Oversight Opens Investigation Into Peltola Campaign Over Second 'Dan Sullivan'
stories.summary:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, ordered an investigation Thursday into Democrat Mary Peltola's Senate campaign. The order followed a New York Times report that people aligned with her campaign helped recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer also opened an investigation, and the Justice Department is reportedly issuing new subpoenas in a probe of the race.

President Trump has called for Peltola's criminal prosecution, calling it "voter fraud at the highest level" at a South Carolina rally. Vice President Vance said the matter should be examined for possible election fraud but did not say whether he agreed with calls to prosecute her. Sen. Lisa Murkowski also accused Peltola's team of ballot manipulation. Sullivan has urged his supporters not to rank Peltola on Alaska's ranked-choice ballot.

Peltola has denied the allegations, and her campaign has said it is focused on lowering costs for Alaskans. Democrats and some election-law observers note that recruiting similarly named candidates is not clearly illegal and that both parties have quietly used little-known candidates in other battlegrounds. Roughly 58,000 early ballots have been cast in Alaska, where the same-name independent appears on the ballot. The race is tight with Election Day on Nov. 3.

stories.headline: US Economy Grew 3.4% in Third Quarter as Inflation Also Accelerated
stories.summary:
The US economy grew at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year, in the last major economic read before next week's midterm elections. Consumer spending rose at a good clip and business investment was up sharply, reflecting the AI boom.

Inflation also picked up. Rising gas prices drove much of the increase as renewed violence in the Middle East has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. Prices also rose outside of fuel costs.

The data highlight the persistent disconnect between economic strength and how Americans feel about it. Economists describe the growth as fragile, and many households continue to struggle with affordability. Gallup polling shows the economy and healthcare are the top issues for voters, alongside the Iran war, and Trump's average approval rating stands near 37 percent in Nate Silver's tracker. The Federal Reserve held rates steady on Wednesday while acknowledging elevated inflation.

stories.headline: Rock Formation Collapse Kills Two at Turkey's Cappadocia Tourist Site
stories.summary:
At least two people were killed and five injured after a rock formation collapsed at a tourist site in Turkey's Cappadocia region on Thursday. One of the "fairy chimney" rock spires reportedly disintegrated at the open-air museum in the town of Göreme, a Unesco World Heritage site.

The collapse occurred near the museum entrance at about 15:15 local time. Nevşehir Governor Hüseyin Kök said the victims' bodies had been recovered from the rubble, and Justice Minister Akın Gürlek confirmed two deaths and five injuries. He warned there could be other victims still trapped, and a search and rescue operation continues.

The cause was not immediately known, though local media reported heavy rain may have triggered the collapse. Cappadocia draws tourists from around the world to see the cone-shaped formations created by volcanic activity.

stories.headline: DoorDash to Acquire Instacart in $17 Billion Deal
stories.summary:
DoorDash announced Thursday that it will acquire Instacart, the grocery delivery company, in a deal valued at about $17 billion. The purchase price is $65 per share. Instacart's board of directors approved the transaction unanimously.

The deal unites two of the largest grocery and food-delivery platforms in the United States. DoorDash said in a statement that Instacart will keep its brand name and that customers will be able to continue using the Instacart app for grocery orders.

The combination would consolidate a significant share of the U.S. delivery market under one company, and it is likely to draw attention from antitrust regulators. The transaction will need regulatory clearance and shareholder approval before it can close, and details on the expected timeline were not included in the initial announcement.

stories.headline: US Sanctions Rwanda's Defense Ministry Over Support for M23 Rebels in Congo
stories.summary:
The United States has imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defense ministry over its alleged support for the M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The measure is intended to pressure Kigali to withdraw its troops and halt support for the rebels. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said, "Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC."

The Treasury alleges the ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23, supplying weapons, equipment, logistics and training. Washington also says minerals from rebel-held territory, including gold and coltan, enter Rwandan supply chains. The US also sanctioned Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a bank serving Rwanda's security services, saying it facilitated tens of millions of dollars in transactions for M23 and its political wing.

The sanctions come months after Rwanda and Congo signed the US-brokered Washington Accords in December 2025, yet fighting has continued since M23 seized Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. Congo's government welcomed the move after President Felix Tshisekedi urged the international community to increase pressure on Rwanda. Rwanda denies backing M23; spokesperson Yolande Makolo said the accords' commitments on neutralizing the FDLR militia remain unmet and that Rwanda is ready to implement the deal alongside Congo.

stories.headline: Putin Calls Musk a 'Real Genius' and Says Russia Is in Close Contact on Satellite Technology
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday that Elon Musk is a "real genius" and that Moscow is in "close contact" with him on satellite technology. He spoke at the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow while discussing Rassvet, Russia's satellite internet project. Putin said contact was needed so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit."

Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 satellites, while trackers show only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites in orbit. The Russian Embassy in South Africa described Rassvet as Russia's Starlink alternative and said it marks the country's first steps in the field. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

The remarks come as US-Russia ties appear to be warming. President Trump said earlier this month he had struck a deal to import Russian diesel to ease fuel prices driven up by the US war with Iran, and then waived certain sanctions on Russia. Ukraine, which relies on Starlink, reported connectivity problems last week that Musk has acknowledged SpaceX caused intentionally.

stories.headline: Sanrio Ends Partnership With Japanese Spy Drama After Chinese Backlash
stories.summary:
Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologized and ended its merchandise partnership with the Japanese TV thriller Vivant after backlash in China. Chinese state media and social media users criticized the show's second season, which depicts Chinese agents torturing a Japanese operative. Sanrio said the show contained elements inconsistent with its core values and pledged to strengthen its review of future collaborations.

China's Foreign Ministry said Thursday the incident should serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan. State-run Global Times said Sanrio should not dance with Japan's right wing and warned it stands to lose far more than short-term sales.

The dispute unfolds amid the worst China-Japan tensions in years, triggered by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's November comments suggesting Japan could use its self-defense forces if China attacked Taiwan. Beijing has since restricted rare earth exports, curbed tourism and reclaimed pandas. Takaichi told parliament she had recorded Vivant episodes to watch. Earlier this week, several Chinese brands dropped footballer Kylian Mbappe over remarks about Mao Zedong.

stories.headline: More Than $405 Million in Ads Flood Top Midterm Races in Final Week
stories.summary:
More than $405 million will be spent on advertising in the final week of the midterm elections across the top 15 House and Senate races, according to AdImpact data as of Wednesday. The figure is expected to keep climbing before Election Day on Tuesday, and it shows where each party sees the best chance to make a late impression on voters.

Republicans are on track to outspend Democrats in Senate races, with at least $143 million in ads from Oct. 27 through Nov. 3. Their largest reservations are $25.5 million for Mike Rogers in Michigan's open seat, $24 million for Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio and $20 million to boost Ken Paxton in Texas. Democrats have reserved more than $119 million for the top 15 races, including $20.3 million for Sherrod Brown in Ohio, $18.5 million in Kansas against Sen. Roger Marshall and $16.4 million in Iowa. The Ohio race has drawn upwards of $500 million in total spending from both parties.

The allocations suggest differing strategic views. Democrats are spending little in Minnesota, where Republicans see a tightening race, and in Florida. Both parties are putting more than $16 million combined into South Carolina, where interim Sen. Darline Graham faces Democrat Annie Andrews. Democrats are spending modestly in North Carolina and Georgia, where their candidates, Roy Cooper and Jon Ossoff, have held sizable polling leads. Republicans are also on pace to outspend Democrats in House races, with nearly $73 million for their top contests.

stories.headline: Update: Leak of Data on More Than 41,000 DHS Personnel Is Third Government Disclosure in a Month
stories.summary:
Details of more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors were published online Wednesday in what appears to be an unprecedented breach. The records include names, work addresses and phone numbers for staff at Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. More than 21,000 of those listed work for CBP and nearly 6,600 for ICE.

The data also named dozens of previously unknown operations, the agents who led them, and technology used in the work, including tools from Cellebrite and Palantir. A group calling itself the Department of Peace said it obtained the profiles through Okta, a single sign-on service, and the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and researcher maia crimew published them in a database called Icepick. The hackers cited Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin's July pledge to turn up the heat on ICE.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is aware of a potential breach and is working to address it, adding that it takes threats against its employees seriously. DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said the aim was to replace anonymity with accountability and that the release was not meant as a directory of every agent. Critics, including commentators writing about national security, have warned the exposure of personnel creates safety and counterintelligence risks, while transparency advocates argue it reveals oversight of covert operations and deportation programs. It is the third government data disclosure in recent weeks.

stories.headline: Ethiopia Acquires 12 Russian Su-35 Jets as Tigray Fighting Intensifies
stories.summary:
Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said while attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow. He called the acquisition a milestone for Ethiopia's defense capacity and said the country plans to buy four S-400 air defense systems. Abiy said the deals were agreed several years ago and the aircraft arrived ahead of schedule.

Abiy described Vladimir Putin as a close friend and said Ethiopia is now the first sub-Saharan African country to own such advanced combat technology. He argued that without such capability, surviving as a country in the region would become difficult. A military analyst told BBC Amharic the purchases suggest preparation for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts, and could help protect assets such as the Renaissance Dam.

The announcement follows fighting that began last month in northern Tigray between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front, with each side accusing the other of violating the 2022 deal that ended the earlier civil war. Ethiopia accuses neighboring Eritrea of backing the TPLF. Ethiopia has relied heavily on drones from Turkey and China in recent conflicts, and Abiy said drones remain important alongside fourth-generation jets.

stories.headline: Conservative Activist James O'Keefe Charged With Unlawful Voting and Identity Theft in Minnesota
stories.summary:
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty charged conservative provocateur James O'Keefe and influencer Cam Higby on Wednesday with felony unlawful voting and identity theft. Prosecutors say the two entered polling places during Minnesota's Aug. 11 primary and identified themselves using the names of registered voters without those voters' knowledge or permission. Moriarty said they also used the names of deceased voters and that investigators do not know where the names came from.

The pair recorded the encounters with hidden cameras while disguised and posted the videos online. O'Keefe said they wore Muslim garb, including a niqab, to expose what he called the lunacy of Minnesota's vouching system, which lets a registered voter vouch for up to eight others. Moriarty said they stopped short of signing the voter oath but that state law bars misrepresenting identity when applying for a ballot. They will receive court summonses rather than be jailed.

Secretary of State Steve Simon, whose office alerted prosecutors, said the men revealed their ignorance of how the laws work and that Minnesota has zero tolerance for lawbreaking at polling places. Neither man immediately commented. The case comes as President Trump and allies press claims of voter fraud and the administration targets Democratic-run states over voter rolls, while Democrats and election officials say such stunts undermine confidence and break the law.

stories.headline: Update: Democrats Lead Generic Ballot by 8 Points as Midterms Near; Judge Rejects DOJ Bid on California Mail Ballots
stories.summary:
With five days until the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the New York Times and Nate Silver polling average shows Democrats leading the generic congressional ballot by 8.2 points as of Oct. 26. President Trump's average approval rating stands at 37 percent in Silver's tracker. Nearly 40 million votes have already been cast, and all 435 House seats and one-third of the Senate are on the ballot.

On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton appointee, declined to order California officials to segregate and not count mail ballots tied to roughly 20,000 people the Justice Department claims are noncitizens. Carter warned the request would "wreak havoc" on elections already underway. Critics called the request legally thin and designed to cast doubt on results, while supporters of the administration framed it as an effort to safeguard election integrity. The Justice Department is also deploying a record 1,000 election monitors nationwide, including to Maine.

In Alaska, the New York Times reported that operatives aligned with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign helped recruit a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan to appear on the ballot against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Peltola's campaign and national Democrats deny involvement. Trump called it "voter fraud at the highest level" and said Peltola should be barred from the race, while Sen. Lisa Murkowski demanded the "truth." Democratic strategists have compared it to past GOP-aligned efforts to boost third-party candidates.

Trump campaigned in Ohio for Sen. Jon Husted, who is in a tight race with Sherrod Brown, while former President Obama rallied in Georgia, saying of Republicans, "These are not serious people." Democrats need to flip four GOP-held Senate seats for a majority, and control may hinge on about a dozen races.

stories.headline: Update: Netanyahu Bloc Leads Israeli Vote Count but Neither Side Reaches Majority
stories.summary:
With roughly 85 to 90 percent of ballots counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and its allies were on track for about 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. That is well short of the 61 needed to govern. The opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot also fell short, even though exit polls had suggested it might lead.

Turnout was the highest in nearly three decades. Arab parties are projected to win 18 to 19 seats, an unprecedented showing, and the two main blocs appear unable to form a government without relying on them. Netanyahu's bloc lost seats but emerged as the largest grouping.

BBC analysts said the most likely outcome is an impasse, potentially leading to new elections. Weeks of coalition negotiations are expected, with ultra-Orthodox draft disputes and Arab party participation among the key obstacles. The result comes amid regional tension, including concerns about a possible renewed war with Iran.

stories.headline: Update: FDA Scientists Opposed HHS Plan to Ease Access to Unproven Peptide Drugs, AP Reports
stories.summary:
Most Food and Drug Administration scientific staff opposed a plan to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., according to six people familiar with its development who spoke to the Associated Press anonymously. The policy document, posted Wednesday by HHS, was driven almost entirely by the department, and FDA staff had limited input.

The policy directs the FDA not to take enforcement action against specialty compounding pharmacies that sell about six wellness peptides, including BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. Under existing rules these substances would be illegal drugs because they have not undergone FDA review for safety and effectiveness. They are promoted in the wellness industry for building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy.

HHS originally wanted a formal regulation adding the peptides to a list of substances deemed safe for compounding. FDA officials said staff had major safety concerns and would not support that, so HHS shifted to an enforcement-discretion approach. Kennedy has called himself a "big fan" of peptides and has described using BPC-157 for a muscle injury. An FDA advisory panel had narrowly recommended easing access to six of seven popular peptides, and an HHS spokesperson did not immediately comment.

stories.headline: El Salvador Sends 2,000 Troops to Haiti Over Four Missing Soldiers
stories.summary:
El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti to find four nationals who went missing nearly two weeks ago, the Salvadoran foreign ministry said Wednesday. President Nayib Bukele informed Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime of the "robust deployment." The troops will also assist security efforts against Haitian gangs.

The four air force technicians, serving with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, were ambushed in an armored vehicle in the Croix-des-Bouquets area, which is controlled by armed groups. No gang has claimed responsibility. Haiti recently handed over four bodies it said were the missing men, but Bukele said they did not match: one was a child and another wore a different country's uniform.

Bukele has threatened to wipe out Haiti's gangs as he did in El Salvador if the men are not released. The Gang Suppression Force has struggled to penetrate gang-held areas, and the UN says more than 5,700 people have been killed in gang violence in Haiti this year. Tensions between the two governments have escalated over the disappearance.
